Drug Elimination metabolism, excretion & the pharmacokinetic parameters

The exit half of ADME, two lectures merged — how the liver metabolises drugs (phases, CYP450, prodrugs), how the kidney and bile excrete them, and the parameters (F, Vd, clearance, half-life, steady state) and kinetics that let you dose by numbers. With worked examples.

§0Orientation · the E of ADME

Drug elimination — the exit

Absorption and distribution got the drug in; elimination gets it out.

This guide merges L5 (metabolism & excretion) and L6 (the parameters that quantify them) to finish the ADME story from the Pharmacokinetics guide. Elimination is the irreversible removal of a drug from the body, and it happens two ways: metabolism (chemically changing the drug) and excretion (physically removing it). The two organs that matter most are the liver (metabolism) and the kidney (excretion).

Reasoning · why the body must eliminate drugs at all

Most drugs are lipid-soluble — that is how they cross membranes to be absorbed and distributed (see the PK guide). But lipid-soluble molecules are passively reabsorbed in the kidney tubule and never leave. So the body's core strategy is to make drugs more water-soluble (metabolism) so the kidney can excrete them. Elimination is really 'convert to water-soluble, then flush out' — the theme that unifies every section below.

Clinical · why elimination sets the dose

Everything about dosing — how much, how often, whether to adjust in disease — is governed by how fast a patient eliminates the drug. Liver or kidney impairment slows elimination, drugs accumulate, and toxicity follows. That is why §4's parameters (clearance, half-life) are not academic: they are the numbers you dose by.

R Recall checklist — orientation
  • Elimination = irreversible removal of a drug, via metabolism and/or excretion.
  • Core strategy: make lipid-soluble drugs water-soluble so the kidney can excrete them.
  • Primary organs: liver (metabolism) and kidney (excretion).
  • Elimination rate determines dose size, frequency, and adjustments in disease.
§1Metabolism · LO2/3

Drug metabolism (biotransformation)

From the Greek metabole = change: enzymes rewrite the drug's chemistry.

Metabolism (biotransformation) is the chemical modification of a drug, usually by an enzyme. Drugs are xenobiotics (foreign chemicals) that the body detoxifies via a well-developed system. The liver is the primary site (also gut wall, kidneys, plasma) — and its first-pass effect was introduced in the PK guide.

§1.1Prodrugs and active metabolites

The product of metabolism is a metabolite — and it is not always less active (Plate 1.1). An active drug may become a less-active, a more-active, or an inactive metabolite; a prodrug (e.g. codeine) is inactive until metabolised into its active form.

Label Key — Prodrug vs active drug
Prodrug
Administered inactive; metabolism switches it on (e.g. codeine → morphine).
Active drug
Already active; metabolism may leave a less-active, more-active or inactive metabolite.
More water-soluble product
Metabolism mostly yields more water-soluble compounds → ready for urine excretion.
Reasoning · why 'metabolism = inactivation' is a trap

It is tempting to equate metabolism with switching a drug off — but codeine is useless until CYP2D6 converts ~10% of it to morphine. So a patient who is a poor CYP2D6 metaboliser gets little pain relief from codeine, while an ultra-rapid metaboliser can reach dangerous morphine levels. Metabolism can turn a drug on, up, down or off — which is exactly why enzyme variation (§2) changes the clinical effect.

§1.2Phase 1 — functionalisation

Metabolism runs in up to two phases, both aimed at decreasing lipid solubility (Plate 1.2). Phase 1 reactions are catabolic — oxidation, reduction or hydrolysis — that introduce or expose a reactive polar functional group, making the drug more water-soluble. A caution: Phase 1 metabolites are sometimes more toxic or carcinogenic than the parent drug.

Label Key — Phase 1 & Phase 2
Phase 1 (functionalisation)
Oxidation/reduction/hydrolysis adds a polar handle — makes the drug more water-soluble (and reactive).
Phase 2 (conjugation)
Attaches a large endogenous molecule to that handle — usually inactivating and very water-soluble.
Drug → metabolite → conjugate
The phases can run in sequence (1 then 2) or independently.
Net effect
Both phases lower lipid solubility so the kidney can excrete the product.
Clinical · when Phase 1 makes things worse — paracetamol

Phase 1 can create a more toxic metabolite. Paracetamol's CYP pathway produces NAPQI, a reactive toxin normally mopped up by Phase 2 conjugation with glutathione. In overdose, glutathione runs out, NAPQI accumulates, and the liver is injured — the reason paracetamol overdose is treated with N-acetylcysteine to replenish glutathione. A perfect illustration that Phase 1 alone is not always 'detox'.

§1.3The cytochrome P450 system

The workhorses of Phase 1 are the cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes — a large family embedded in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum of hepatocytes. To reach them a drug must cross the plasma membrane (non-polar drugs cross more readily). CYPs are named CYP + family number + subfamily letter + gene number (e.g. CYP3A4). Crucially, just five — CYP1A2, 3A4, 2D6, 2C9, 2C19 — handle over 50% of small-molecule drug metabolism.

Reasoning · why a handful of enzymes cause most drug interactions

Because so much metabolism funnels through a few CYPs, anything that induces or inhibits one of them (§2) shifts the levels of many drugs at once. CYPs also have overlapping substrate specificities, so one drug can be handled by several CYPs and one CYP by many drugs — a dense web where a single inhibitor (grapefruit juice on CYP3A4) can raise the levels of dozens of medicines.

Memory hook · the big-five CYPs

"1A2, 2C9, 2C19, 2D6, 3A4 — the big five."

Five enzymes do most of the work: 1A2, 2C9, 2C19, 2D6, 3A4 — the '2C' pair flanked by the bookends 1A2 and 3A4, plus 2D6. 3A4 is the busiest (and the grapefruit-sensitive one).

§1.4Phase 2 — conjugation

Phase 2 reactions are anabolic: a transferase enzyme conjugates (attaches) the drug to an endogenous molecule (e.g. glucuronic acid, sulfate, glutathione). The products are usually inactive and highly water-soluble, and it happens mainly in the liver. Phase 1 and Phase 2 may be sequential or simultaneous. The opioid pathway (Plate 1.3) shows both at work.

Label Key — Opioid metabolism
Codeine → morphine (CYP2D6)
A Phase 1 oxidation that activates the prodrug — the source of codeine's effect.
Glucuronidation (Phase 2)
Morphine is conjugated to morphine-glucuronides — mostly inactivating and water-soluble.
Multiple parallel routes
Shows overlapping enzymes and both phases operating on one drug family.
Water-soluble end-products
Ready for renal excretion (§3).

§1.5Stereoselectivity

Stereoisomers differ only in the spatial arrangement of their atoms, yet enzymes treat them differently. Many important drugs are stereoisomer mixtures (e.g. warfarin): the isomers can differ in both effect (pharmacodynamics) and metabolism (pharmacokinetics), and sometimes toxicity is linked to only one isomer.

Clinical · warfarin's two faces

Warfarin is given as a 50:50 mix of R- and S-enantiomers, but S-warfarin is ~3–5× more potent and is metabolised by a different CYP (2C9) than R-warfarin. So a CYP2C9 inhibitor raises the more potent isomer selectively — a big, and dangerous, change in anticoagulation from a 'small' stereochemical detail.

R Recall checklist — metabolism
  • Biotransformation = enzymatic chemical change; liver is primary (also gut, kidney, plasma).
  • Metabolites can be less active, more active, or inactive; prodrugs (codeine) are activated by metabolism.
  • Phase 1 — catabolic (oxidation/reduction/hydrolysis), adds a polar group, ↑ water solubility, sometimes ↑ toxicity.
  • CYP450 — ER-bound family; CYP1A2/3A4/2D6/2C9/2C19 do >50% of small-molecule metabolism.
  • Phase 2 — anabolic conjugation by transferases; usually inactive, very water-soluble.
  • Stereoselectivity — isomers (warfarin) differ in PD, PK and toxicity.
§2Factors · LO4

What changes metabolism

Genes, other drugs, dose and disease all move the CYP dial.

Metabolic rate varies enormously between people and situations — the main reasons are genetics, enzyme induction/inhibition, concentration, and disease.

  • Genetic polymorphisms — inherited variation in enzymes (e.g. "slow vs fast acetylators") can profoundly change drug levels.
  • Induction & inhibition of CYP450 — other drugs speed up or slow down the enzymes (table below).
  • Concentration-dependent biotransformation — enzymes can saturate (the basis of zero-order kinetics, §5).
  • Disease — liver disease is especially important, since the liver is the main metaboliser.
Drugs that induce or inhibit key CYP enzymes (L5 slide 17)
CYPInducersInhibitorsSubstrates
CYP1A2Omeprazole; tobacco smokingCiprofloxacin; fluvoxamineWarfarin; olanzapine
CYP2D6—Bupropion; fluoxetine; paroxetine; terbinafineCodeine; flecainide; oxycodone; amitriptyline
CYP3A4/5Carbamazepine; St John's wort; rifampicin; efavirenzClarithromycin; fluconazole; grapefruit juiceWarfarin; atorvastatin; clopidogrel; codeine; diazepam
Reasoning · induction vs inhibition act in opposite directions and timescales

An inhibitor blocks the enzyme immediately, so a substrate's level rises fast (toxicity risk) — grapefruit juice on CYP3A4 raises statin and diazepam levels within a day. An inducer makes the cell build more enzyme, so the substrate's level falls slowly over days–weeks (treatment failure) — rifampicin or St John's wort lowers levels of the pill, warfarin and many others. Same enzyme, opposite effect, different speed.

Clinical · the codeine + fluoxetine trap

Codeine needs CYP2D6 to become morphine. Give a CYP2D6 inhibitor (fluoxetine, paroxetine) alongside and codeine can't be activated — the patient gets no analgesia. It is the mirror of the ultra-rapid metaboliser who over-produces morphine. Reading the table's 'inhibitor' and 'substrate' columns together predicts these interactions.

A special case is alcohol (Plate 2.1), whose hepatic metabolism both illustrates enzyme handling and, at higher doses, saturates (zero-order kinetics, §5).

Label Key — Alcohol metabolism
Alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH)
Main enzyme: ethanol → acetaldehyde (the toxic, hangover-causing intermediate).
CYP2E1 (MEOS)
An inducible microsomal route that becomes important at high/chronic intake.
Acetaldehyde → acetate
Aldehyde dehydrogenase clears the toxic intermediate (blocked by disulfiram).
Saturable pathways
At ordinary doses the enzymes are saturated → alcohol shows zero-order elimination (§5).
R Recall checklist — factors affecting metabolism
  • Genetic polymorphisms — e.g. slow vs fast acetylators — shift drug levels.
  • Inhibition → substrate rises fast (toxicity); induction → substrate falls slowly (failure).
  • Know CYP3A4 (grapefruit, clarithromycin, rifampicin) and CYP2D6 (codeine, fluoxetine).
  • Concentration can saturate enzymes (→ zero-order); liver disease impairs metabolism.
  • Alcohol — ADH/CYP2E1; saturable → zero-order elimination.
§3Excretion · LO5

Excretion

Removing the drug (or its metabolite) from the body — mostly through the kidney.

Most drugs are excreted by the kidney (renal, in urine) — either unchanged or as polar metabolites. Most metabolites are inactive, but 25–30% of drugs are excreted mainly in the active (unchanged) form; for these, renal impairment causes accumulation and toxicity.

Other routes of excretion

Routes of excretion (L5 slide 20)
RouteWhat it handles
Renal (urine)Main route — unchanged drug or polar metabolites
HepatobiliaryLarger molecules (MW > 350) and many drug conjugates
Pulmonary (lungs)Highly volatile or gaseous agents (e.g. anaesthetics, alcohol)
Sweat, saliva, tearsMinor routes
Breast milkMinor by amount, but clinically important for the infant

§3.1Renal excretion — three processes

Renal handling is the net of three processes:

  1. Glomerular filtration — drugs cross the glomerular filter freely unless highly bound to plasma protein (bound drug is too big to filter).
  2. Active tubular secretion — carriers actively pump drug into the tubule: organic cation transporters (OCTs) for basic (protonated) drugs, organic anion transporters (OATs) for acidic drugs.
  3. Passive tubular reabsorption — lipid-soluble drugs diffuse back out of the tubule with reabsorbed water, so they are not efficiently excreted (the whole reason metabolism exists).
Reasoning · why protein binding and lipid solubility control renal excretion

Two of the three processes are gatekeepers. Protein binding keeps a drug in the blood — bound drug can't be filtered — so a highly bound drug leaves slowly. Lipid solubility lets a filtered drug be reabsorbed straight back, so it never actually leaves. This is why the body first makes drugs water-soluble (§1): a water-soluble, unbound drug is filtered and stays filtered.

§3.2Hepatobiliary excretion & the enterohepatic circulation

The liver also secretes drugs into bile (via OCTs, OATs and P-glycoproteins), which carries them to the small intestine (Plate 3.1). There, a drug can be reabsorbed to be excreted by the kidney, or recirculate between gut and liver until finally excreted in urine or faeces. Glucuronide conjugates can be split by gut bacteria, freeing the drug to be reabsorbed.

Label Key — Enterohepatic circulation
Liver → bile
Drugs/conjugates are secreted into bile via OCT/OAT/P-gp transporters.
Bile → small intestine
Delivered to the gut lumen.
Reabsorption
Gut bacteria can cleave glucuronides, freeing drug that is then reabsorbed into the portal blood.
Recirculation
The loop prolongs a drug's stay in the body — a longer effective half-life.
Clinical · why enterohepatic recycling matters

Recirculation prolongs drug action (e.g. it helps sustain the effect of some drugs) but also means gut events change drug levels — antibiotics that kill gut flora can stop the deconjugation step, reducing reabsorption of the oestrogen in the combined pill and (rarely) contributing to contraceptive failure. It is also exploited therapeutically: activated charcoal interrupts the loop to speed clearance in some overdoses.

§3.3Drug interactions at excretion

Excretion can be manipulated (deliberately or accidentally) by:

  • Altering protein binding — displacing a drug frees more to be filtered.
  • Inhibiting tubular secretion — classically, probenecid blocks the OAT that secretes penicillin, keeping penicillin levels high for longer.
  • Altering urine flow / pH — diuretics, and drugs that alkalinise or acidify the urine, change reabsorption (the basis of urinary alkalinisation in aspirin overdose).

A real drug's overall elimination combines all of this (Plate 3.2).

Label Key — A real elimination profile
~2/3 metabolic degradation
The liver (CYP3A4/2J2) transforms much of the dose.
~1/3 renal excretion of unchanged drug
Active drug removed directly by the kidney — so renal impairment raises levels.
Hepatobiliary / faecal route
The remainder leaves via bile/faeces.
Multiple routes = robustness
Splitting elimination across organs buffers against any one organ failing.
R Recall checklist — excretion
  • Renal is the main route; 25–30% of drugs leave mainly unchanged (active) → renal impairment causes toxicity.
  • Other routes: hepatobiliary (MW>350, conjugates), pulmonary (volatiles), sweat/saliva/tears, breast milk.
  • Renal 3 processes — filtration (not if protein-bound), active secretion (OCT/OAT), passive reabsorption (lipid-soluble).
  • Enterohepatic circulation recycles drug (bile → gut → reabsorption) → prolongs action.
  • Interactions — probenecid + penicillin (blocks secretion); urine pH/flow changes reabsorption.
§4PK parameters · L6 LO1/2

The pharmacokinetic parameters

Four numbers govern drug disposition: bioavailability, volume of distribution, clearance and half-life.

L6 turns the ADME story into numbers you can dose by. The four most important are bioavailability (F), volume of distribution (Vd), clearance (CL) and half-life (t½) — plus the steady state they combine to produce.

§4.1Bioavailability (F)

Bioavailability is the fraction (F) of a dose that reaches the systemic circulation unaltered (Plate 4.1). IV drug is 100% available (F = 1.0); oral drugs are less, cut down by poor absorption and first-pass metabolism.

Label Key — Bioavailability (F)
F = fraction reaching circulation
1.0 for IV; <1.0 for oral by the amount lost.
First-pass metabolism
Oral drug traverses gut wall + liver before the systemic circulation, losing a fraction.
AUC (area under the curve)
F is measured by comparing oral vs IV AUC of plasma concentration.

§4.2Volume of distribution (Vd)

Vd is an apparent volume — it does not correspond to a real body volume (Plate 4.2). It is the volume of fluid into which a drug appears to be diluted: Vd = amount of drug in body (mg) ÷ plasma concentration (mg/L). Factors: age, gender, body composition, disease. Minimal tissue binding → Vd close to plasma volume; heavy tissue binding → a very large Vd.

Label Key — Apparent volume of distribution
Vd = dose ÷ plasma concentration
A high plasma concentration for a given dose means a small Vd (drug stayed in blood).
Small Vd
Drug held in plasma (large, protein-bound, water-soluble) → Vd near plasma volume.
Large Vd
Drug hides in tissues (lipophilic) → plasma level low → Vd can exceed total body water.
Worked example · initial concentration & Vd

A 500 mg IV dose gives a measured plasma concentration of 25 mg/L. What is the apparent volume of distribution?

  1. State the relationship: Vd = amount in body ÷ plasma concentration (C0).
  2. Substitute: Vd = 500 mg ÷ 25 mg/L.
  3. Simplify: Vd = 20 L — larger than plasma (~3 L), so the drug distributes into tissues.

Answer: Vd = 20 L (an apparent volume; rearrange to find C0 = Dose ÷ Vd for a target level).

§4.3Elimination half-life (t½)

t½ is the time for the plasma concentration (Cp) to fall by half (Plate 4.3). It sets duration of action, dosing frequency and time to steady state. It is directly proportional to Vd and inversely proportional to clearance, and a drug is essentially completely eliminated after ~6 half-lives.

Label Key — Half-life & AUC
t½
The time for plasma concentration to halve — constant in first-order kinetics.
AUC (area under the curve)
Total drug exposure over time; used to measure bioavailability.
Absorption vs elimination phases
The rising then falling limbs of the plasma curve after an oral dose.
~6 half-lives
Time for near-complete elimination of the drug.
Worked example · elimination rate constant from half-life

A drug has a half-life of 4 hours. Find its elimination rate constant (kel) and roughly when it is cleared.

  1. Relationship: kel = 0.693 ÷ t½ (0.693 = ln2).
  2. Substitute: kel = 0.693 ÷ 4 h = 0.173 h⁻¹ — ~17.3% of the remaining drug leaves each hour.
  3. Near-complete elimination ≈ 6 × t½ = 24 h. Also CL = kel × Vd links the three parameters.

Answer: kel ≈ 0.173 h⁻¹; essentially cleared by ~24 h.

§4.4Clearance (CL)

Clearance is arguably the most important PK parameter: the volume of plasma completely cleared of drug per unit time (L/h). CLtot = rate of elimination ÷ plasma concentration (Cp). Total clearance (all routes) determines the maintenance dose and rate of administration. For most drugs the rate of elimination is directly proportional to concentration (first-order, §5).

Reasoning · why clearance, not half-life, sets the maintenance dose

Half-life feels like the master number, but it is a derived one — t½ = 0.693 × Vd ÷ CL. Clearance is the true measure of the body's capacity to remove drug, independent of how much is in the body. To keep a steady level you must replace exactly what is cleared, so the maintenance-dose rate = CL × target concentration. Change Vd (e.g. fluid shifts) and t½ changes without clearance moving — which is why dosing is built on clearance.

§4.5Steady-state concentration (Css)

With repeated dosing, drug accumulates until rate in = rate out — the steady state (Plate 4.4), reached after 3–5 half-lives. Css = rate of administration ÷ CLtot; for oral dosing, Css = (F × Dose) ÷ (CLtot × dosing interval T).

Label Key — Steady-state concentration
Steady state
Where input rate equals elimination rate; plasma level plateaus.
3–5 half-lives
Time to reach steady state with regular dosing (independent of dose size).
Loading dose
A larger first dose can reach the target immediately when 3–5 t½ is too long to wait.
Css ∝ F·Dose / (CL·T)
Raise dose or F, or lengthen clearance/interval, to shift the plateau.
Worked example · oral steady-state concentration

A drug is given orally: F = 0.7, Dose = 200 mg every 8 h, total clearance CLtot = 6 L/h. Find the average steady-state concentration.

  1. Relationship (oral): Css = (F × Dose) ÷ (CLtot × T).
  2. Substitute: Css = (0.7 × 200 mg) ÷ (6 L/h × 8 h).
  3. Simplify: Css = 140 mg ÷ 48 L = 2.9 mg/L.

Answer: Css ≈ 2.9 mg/L; steady state is reached after 3–5 half-lives regardless of this value.

Memory hook · half-life rules of thumb

"3–5 to steady state, 6 to gone."

3–5 to arrive, 6 to leave. Steady state is reached after 3–5 half-lives of regular dosing; a drug is essentially cleared 6 half-lives after the last dose.

R Recall checklist — PK parameters
  • Bioavailability F — fraction reaching circulation unaltered; IV = 1.0; oral cut by absorption + first-pass.
  • Vd (apparent) = amount in body ÷ plasma conc; large Vd = tissue-hidden drug.
  • t½ — time for Cp to halve; ∝ Vd, ∝ 1/CL; ~6 t½ to eliminate; kel = 0.693/t½.
  • Clearance — plasma volume cleared per time; sets the maintenance dose (rate = CL × target).
  • Steady state — rate in = rate out, reached in 3–5 t½; oral Css = F·Dose/(CL·T).
§5Kinetics · L6 LO3

First-order vs zero-order elimination

Most drugs clear a constant fraction; a few clear a constant amount.

The last idea is how concentration falls over time — and there are two patterns (Plate 5.1).

First-order vs zero-order (saturation) kinetics
First-order (most drugs)Zero-order (saturation)
Rate of eliminationProportional to concentrationConstant, independent of concentration
Amount removed / timeA constant fraction per unit timeA constant amount per unit time
ClearanceConstantDecreases as concentration rises
CauseEnzymes not saturatedSaturated protein binding, hepatic metabolism or renal transport
ExamplesThe majority of drugsAlcohol, phenytoin
Label Key — Elimination kinetics
First-order (curve)
Concentration falls exponentially; a straight line on a log plot; constant t½.
Zero-order (straight line)
Concentration falls linearly; no constant half-life; a straight line on a linear plot.
Fraction vs amount
First-order removes a set % each interval; zero-order removes a set mg each interval.
Reasoning · why saturation flips fraction into amount

First-order works because enzymes have spare capacity — double the drug and they remove double the amount (a constant fraction). Once the drug saturates the enzymes (or transporters), they are already working flat out: they can only remove a fixed amount per unit time no matter how much more you add. So clearance falls as concentration climbs, and small dose increases cause disproportionately large — sometimes toxic — jumps in level.

Label Key — Zero-order / saturation
Linear decline
A fixed amount of drug is removed per unit time, so the curve is a straight line.
Saturated pathway
Protein binding, metabolism or transport is maxed out.
Alcohol / phenytoin
Classic examples — why one extra drink or a small phenytoin dose rise can overshoot dangerously.
Clinical · why phenytoin is dangerous near the top of its range

Phenytoin shows zero-order kinetics at therapeutic doses. Because clearance falls as the level rises, a small dose increase can cause a large, toxic rise in plasma level — the reason phenytoin needs careful monitoring and tiny dose adjustments. Alcohol behaves the same way: you sober up at a fixed rate regardless of how much you drank.

§5.1The two-compartment model

Finally, many drugs behave as if the body were two compartments (Plate 5.3): a central compartment (plasma + well-perfused organs) and a peripheral compartment (slower tissues). After an IV dose the plasma level shows a fast distribution phase then a slower elimination phase.

Label Key — Two-compartment model
Central compartment
Plasma + well-perfused tissues; where dose enters and drug is measured.
Peripheral compartment
Slower-equilibrating tissues; drug distributes in and back out.
Distribution then elimination
The early steep fall is redistribution; the later shallow fall is true elimination.
Why it matters
Explains why a plasma curve has two slopes and why loading vs maintenance dosing differ.
Memory hook · first vs zero order

First-order = Fraction (a fixed % leaves; constant half-life). Zero-order = 'Zero cares about concentration' (a fixed amount leaves; no constant half-life). Alcohol & phenytoin are the zero-order pair.

R Recall checklist — kinetics
  • First-order (most drugs) — rate ∝ concentration; constant fraction/unit time; constant clearance & t½.
  • Zero-order — constant amount/unit time; clearance falls with concentration; alcohol, phenytoin.
  • Saturation of binding, metabolism or transport causes zero-order → small dose rises can be toxic.
  • Two-compartment model — central (plasma) vs peripheral (tissue); distribution then elimination phases.
  • PK matters for drug development, individualised dosing, dose adjustment and loading doses.
